articles.title: ‘Calculated, intentional act’: SIT says Gurgaon woman biker was deliberately rammed by car
articles.summary: GURGAON: The Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the road rage incident involving female biker Shivani Chauhan found that accused Kalyan Baisla
articles.body: GURGAON: The Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the road rage incident involving female biker Shivani Chauhan found that accused Kalyan Baisla deliberately rammed his car into her motorcycle after misbehaving with her.Police said all charges in the FIR, including attempt to murder, are likely to be retained in the chargesheet.The incident took place on September 13 and was captured on Shivani's helmet-mounted camera as well as a camera belonging to a fellow biker. It sparked outrage after she shared the video on social media.Shivani, alias Siya, a 27-year-old resident of Delhi's Kalkaji, was travelling with her friends from Golf Course Road towards Extension Road when the accused, driving a white car, allegedly followed them and made obscene gestures.His vehicle then rammed into her motorcycle from the side before fleeing the scene. The impact knocked her off the bike and sent her skidding on the road.After his arrest, Baisla admitted that the collision was his fault but denied hitting her deliberately, claiming he "lost control near a U-turn".However, the SIT concluded that "this was not an accident, but a calculated, intentional act", a senior police officer said.The investigation found that the accused car driver, Kalyan Baisla, had "deliberately rammed his vehicle into the female biker's motorcycle following an act of misbehaviour", the officer said.The five-member SIT, headed by ACP (Crimes Against Women) Sushila, recently submitted its report to the police commissioner."The SIT has prepared a draft of the charge sheet. The charge sheet will be filed in court within a week, in accordance with the sections of law applied in the FIR," ACP (Crimes Against Women) Sushila said.Following Shivani's complaint, Gurgaon police registered an FIR under Sections 78 (physical and digital stalking), 79 (use any word, sound, gesture, object, or intrusion of privacy with the intent to insult the modesty of a woman), 109 (attempt to murder) and 3(5) (common intention) of the BNS.The SIT was constituted by police commissioner Sibash Kaviraj following a notice from the Haryana Commission for Women.Four people were in the car at the time of the incident. Baisla and his cousin Lavnish were seated in the front.Gurgaon Police arrested Baisla and Lavnish in Rajasthan's Rajgarh, Dausa, on September 15. articles.body: The first course in a new online-learning initiative at a US university was a sophomore-level electrical engineering class on circuits and electronics, a subject that students on campus often find difficult. Unlike a recorded lecture, it offered weekly video lessons, graded homework, online laboratories, exams that counted toward a certificate and a discussion forum and anyone with an internet connection could sign up for free. The course was a prototype, built to test whether much of a campus course could be delivered to learners anywhere and its organizers expected far fewer participants than actually registered. It became both the starting point for a larger platform and a source of data on how people learn in an open online course. The sections below follow the course’s launch, its enrollment and completion numbers, and the research it produced.MITx opens with one course on March 5, 2012MIT unveiled the MITx platform in December 2011 with one course, 6.002x Circuits and Electronics, taught by Anant Agarwal, who later became edX CEO, Class Central recounts. 6.002x launched on March 5, 2012 and ran through June 8, about 14 weeks. Agarwal, in an MIT YouTube video, named his teaching colleagues as Gerry Sussman, Chris Terman, Piotr Mitros and Jacob White. According to Class Central, everyone who registered got free access to an embedded textbook, one of whose authors was Agarwal. In May 2012, Harvard joined the effort and MITx became edX.Planned for 2,000 sign-ups, nearly 155,000 registered from more than 160 countriesMIT’s March 5, 2012 news release said more than 90,000 people had signed up for the prototype course since registration opened in February, far above the original estimate of 2,000 students. Technology Review quoted Agarwal as saying that 10,000 sign-ups would be a fantastic success. Registration kept growing during the run and by the end almost 155,000 people from more than 160 countries had registered, according to the MIT News account that ACM carries. Agarwal compared that figure with the number of students he estimated might have taken the course at MIT over 40 years.From 23,349 first problem set attempts to 7,157 certificatesThe attrition shows what registering meant. Of the 154,763 students who registered, 23,349 tried the first problem set, 10,547 made it to the midterm, 9,318 passed it, 8,240 took the final and 7,157 earned a certificate, according to the 2013 paper discussed below. MIT News also reports that a 15-year-old student in Mongolia was one of 341 students to score full marks on the final exam. Access to the course was free, but the certificate process evolved over time. MIT announced on February 13, 2012, that students who mastered the prototype course would receive a certificate free of charge, while future MITx courses would charge a modest fee. Students needed at least 60 points to earn the honor code certificate.A 2013 paper on edX’s first MOOC, written by six researchersThat paper appeared in Research & Practice in Assessment and is titled Studying Learning in the Worldwide Classroom: Research into edX’s First MOOC. Lori Breslow and five co-authors report that the course consisted of video lectures, problem sets, online labs and forums. The course generated a rich data set on how learners used the platform. The first stage of the research measured the time students spent on each tool and the second stage aimed to build a profile of who the students were and how their background and capability related to achievement and persistence.A paper from the course team: designed to be content-identical to MIT’s sophomore coursePiotr Mitros and colleagues, including Agarwal, wrote Teaching electronic circuits online: Lessons from MITx’s 6.002x on edX, which describes the online course as content-identical to the sophomore-level Circuits and Electronics course taken by residential MIT students. Those who managed to accumulate enough points were issued an honor code certificate by MITx.After its initial spring 2012 run, 6.002x was offered again in fall 2012 and spring 2013, according to the above-mentioned study by Breslow and colleagues. Class Central reported that edX shut down the original platform on March 15, 2017, and moved the roughly 155,000 original registrants to an invitation-only alumni version of the course.You use AI every day. articles.title: London homeowner ordered to repay £225,000 to Thames Water after High Court finds she claimed her flood-hit home was unsaleable despite selling it for £780,000
articles.summary: A London homeowner has been ordered to repay £225,000 to Thames Water after the High Court found that she pursued a compensation claim describing her
articles.body: A London homeowner has been ordered to repay £225,000 to Thames Water after the High Court found that she pursued a compensation claim describing her flood-hit property as unsaleable even though she had already sold the property. Karen Imber’s home in Woodford Green, Essex, suffered sewage flooding in 2006, 2007 and 2014.According to International Comparative Legal Guides (ICLG), she brought a claim against the water company for losses caused by the flooding and agreed to a £225,000 settlement in September 2023.However, Thames Water later discovered that Imber had accepted an offer of £780,000 for the property before mediation and completed the sale on 3 August 2023. On 23 October 2026, the High Court rescinded the settlement after finding that the claim involved fraudulent misrepresentation and dishonesty.How did a house sale lead to a £225,000 Thames Water repayment orderDeputy Master Marzec granted summary judgment in favour of Thames Water after finding no real prospect that Thames Water would fail to establish misrepresentation, reliance and dishonesty. Imber had claimed that she was trapped in the property because it was unsaleable. However, she had already accepted an offer to sell the house before the mediation and completed the sale on 3 August 2023.The court found that the completed sale fundamentally changed the factual basis of her claim for a reduction in property value. Thames Water had agreed to pay £225,000 on 6 September 2023 without being informed that the property had been sold. The judge rescinded the settlement agreement and ordered Imber to repay the full amount.Repeated sewage flooding led to a second Thames Water claimImber’s home in Woodford Green, Essex, was flooded by sewage water in 2006 and 2007. She sued Thames Water, and those proceedings concluded in 2013 with a £500,000 settlement agreement. The property flooded again in 2014, prompting her to bring another claim against the company for uninsured losses caused by the flooding. Thames Water denied liability but continued to engage in correspondence.During mediation in 2023, Imber said she was trapped in the property and described it as unsaleable. An expert report valued the property at £817,000 on the hypothetical basis that it had never suffered flooding. Her additional claims covered relocation costs, increased insurance and mortgage premiums, legal costs, distress and inconvenience, totalling £144,000.How did a £780,000 house sale lead to a Thames Water fraud claimThames Water disputed that the flooding had reduced the property's market value and argued that it could be sold for its full market value. Nevertheless, the company agreed to the £225,000 settlement on 6 September 2023. It later discovered that Imber had accepted a £780,000 offer before the mediation and completed the sale on 3 August 2023.The company then brought a claim alleging fraudulent misrepresentation. Imber denied acting dishonestly or fraudulently by failing to correct her statement during mediation. Deputy Master Marzec held that describing the property as unsaleable implied that it had not been sold and that there was no prospect of a future sale. Those implied representations became false when the transaction was completed.High Court orders homeowner to repay £225,000 to Thames WaterDeputy Master Marzec found that Thames Water had relied on the false representation when agreeing to the settlement. He said it was impossible to imagine that the company would have reached the same agreement if Imber had corrected the statement. The judge applied the honesty test established by the Supreme Court in Ivey v Genting Casinos (2017), considering the defendant’s knowledge and beliefs before assessing her conduct against the standards of ordinary decent people.He held that continuing to pursue and settle a claim based on a property being unsaleable, without disclosing that it had been sold, would plainly be regarded as dishonest. The court found no real prospect that Thames Water would fail to establish misrepresentation, reliance and dishonesty. The settlement was rescinded, and Imber was ordered to repay £225,000.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information. articles.title: An Indiana couple paid a contractor with cheques and a Ford F-350 truck for home repairs, but he made roof trusses in his backyard; on October 26 a court made him personally liable for an $82,020 judgment
articles.summary: A home renovation project can turn into a costly dispute when promised materials never arrive and the work fails to meet the contract.
articles.body: A home renovation project can turn into a costly dispute when promised materials never arrive and the work fails to meet the contract. In Indiana, a couple who hired a contractor to repair a house and garage secured an $82,020 judgment against his construction company after a court found that it had breached the contract and made material and fraudulent misrepresentations. On October 26, 2026, an appeals court ruled that the contractor himself could also be held personally liable.According to the Indiana Court of Appeals’ memorandum decision in Robert Burgner, et al. v. Jeremy Swenson, et al., available on Justia, the contractor had accepted cheques and a Ford F-350 truck as part of the arrangement, but the promised manufactured roof trusses were never supplied as agreed. The appellate court reversed the lower court’s refusal to impose personal liability on Jeremy Swenson, concluding that he could not use his company as a shield against responsibility for fraudulent conduct in which he had personally participated.Couple hired contractor for house and garage repairsThe dispute began in early 2022, when Robert Burgner contacted Swenson about repairs and improvements to a property on Harrison Street in Veedersburg, Indiana. The property included a house and a garage that had been unoccupied for several years. Swenson operated a construction business called SwenCrest, LLC, of which he was the sole member. He prepared a written estimate on the company’s letterhead, outlining the planned work and estimated material costs. The contract, signed in April 2022, quoted a total of $25,286.75, with labour costs listed as zero. The parties agreed that Burgner would transfer ownership of a 2005 Ford F-350 truck as payment for the work.The agreement specified the use of manufactured roof trusses. The couple also made additional payments by cheque to cover materials, including $9,000 in April 2022 and $6,000 in July that year. The money was intended to pay for trusses and other construction materials, including roofing supplies.Manufactured roof trusses were never deliveredBy July 2022, Burgner discovered that the roof trusses had not been ordered. He and Swenson subsequently visited Ferguson Lumber, where Swenson placed an order for the materials, which were expected to arrive in November. However, the lumber supplier later cancelled the order. According to an employee of Ferguson Lumber, the cancellation occurred because Swenson had an unpaid account with the supplier.In September 2022, Swenson took possession of the Ford F-350, and Burgner transferred the vehicle’s title documents, assigning the truck to SwenCrest, LLC. The following month, the couple issued another cheque for $2,023.36 at Swenson’s direction, making it payable to him personally. Swenson later acknowledged that he deposited the cheque electronically and then cashed it at the couple’s bank. He repaid the amount about 30 days after Burgner raised the issue.In November, Burgner visited Swenson’s home to investigate the missing trusses. There, he discovered trusses being constructed in the contractor’s backyard for the couple’s project. Burgner rejected them because the contract specified manufactured trusses rather than the ones being made on-site. The couple also encountered delays in the remaining work. Swenson claimed that he had obtained a building permit, but records from the Town of Veedersburg showed that neither he nor his company had applied for one for the property.Construction company ordered to pay more than $82,000In June 2023, the couple terminated the contract and demanded repayment of $17,000 paid for materials that had not been ordered, along with $10,000 for damage caused by faulty workmanship. They subsequently filed a lawsuit against Swenson, his wife and the construction business, alleging breach of contract, fraud and other claims.During the proceedings, evidence raised questions about the company’s financial records and its handling of funds. Swenson acknowledged that some personal expenses had appeared in the company’s bank account. He also could definitively identify only about $500 in receipts as relating to the Burgners’ project. In July 2025, the trial court found that SwenCrest had breached the contract and made material and fraudulent misrepresentations. It awarded the couple damages, including amounts they had paid, costs for repairs and further work by another contractor, estimated future repair costs, attorney’s fees and filing fees.After trebling the damages, the court entered judgment against SwenCrest, Inc., for $82,020.08, plus costs. However, it declined to hold Swenson personally liable, finding that the circumstances did not justify piercing the corporate veil. The couple challenged that part of the decision.Appeals court says contractor can be held personally liableThe Indiana Court of Appeals concluded that Swenson could be held personally liable for his own participation in the fraudulent conduct, even without piercing the corporate veil. The judges explained that corporate officers and members of limited liability companies are generally protected from responsibility for business debts. However, that protection does not prevent them from being held personally liable for wrongful conduct in which they directly participate.The court noted that Swenson was the sole member of the LLC and the person who dealt with the couple throughout the transaction. He accepted their payments, failed to purchase materials as promised, did not disclose the cancellation of the truss order and attempted to construct the trusses himself despite the contract’s specifications. The court therefore reversed the decision refusing to hold Swenson personally liable and remanded the case with instructions to enter judgment against both Swenson and SwenCrest, Inc.The ruling does not mean that business owners are automatically responsible for every company debt. Instead, it reinforces the distinction between liability arising from a company’s obligations and liability arising from an individual’s own fraudulent conduct. The October 26 decision was issued as a memorandum decision and is not binding precedent under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D), although it may be cited for persuasive value.You use AI every day. articles.title: M25 turning 40: Keeping Britain's busiest motorway moving
articles.summary: Highway workers recall some of the unexpected incidents they have encountered over the years.
articles.body:
Sometimes referred to as "The Road to Hell" or "Europe's largest car park", the M25 remains an essential part of Britain's transport network.

Since it officially opened on 29 October 1986, many workers over the years have contributed to the establishment and maintenance of the UK's busiest motorway.

Chris Nutton, traffic officer for National Highways, said: "We have days when it runs very smoothly and we have days when all hell can break loose."

His colleague Esther Martin added that aside from dealing with daily incidents like vehicle breakdowns, they have encountered some unexpected ones like bolting horses.

Nutton recalled a driver discarding a lit cigarette from a car window and unwittingly setting ablaze the lorry load of hay bales behind them.

He added there were instances of drivers falling asleep while stuck in traffic jams and an extraordinary array of items strewn across the tarmac.

"During the festive period we have previously come across presents that have fallen out of car roof boxes and spread across the carriageway," Martin added.

"Sometimes we have been able to reunite them with owners, but sometimes they've ended up under lorry wheels."

Martin said on other occasions, items including wheelbarrows, bicycles, canoes and even a longbow were found.

Former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher cut the ribbon to mark the completion of the M25 on 29 October 1986, hailing it as a "magnificent achievement".

The 117-mile motorway, which runs through Kent, Surrey, Greater London, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire and Essex, quickly attracted huge numbers of motorists.

This has led to chronic congestion despite decades of efforts to keep traffic moving, including widening lanes, upgrading junctions and introducing "smart motorways".

Retired civil engineer Tony Ferris was one of the original team helping to create the M25.

He said he was proud of what they had achieved.

"It was a momentous piece of work over many years. I started working on it in 1980."

When asked if he believed the motorway deserved the criticism it sometimes received, he replied "I don't think so".

"When it runs smoothly and nicely it's great. It's almost a victim of its own success - everybody wants to use it," he said.

Since 2009, a consortium called Connect Plus has been managing the M25 after winning a 30-year £6.2bn contract.

Simon Wilkinson, commercial manager, said: "It's understandable it gets a bad rap sometimes.

"However it is because so many people want to use the M25 and we'd miss if it wasn't there."

articles.title: Sheffield project sells pre-loved clothes for as little as 50p
articles.summary: The Echo project was partly set up in response to the cost of living crisis, say organisers.
articles.body:
A community project is offering clothing for as little as 50p to help families who are struggling with the cost of living.

The Echo project, based at York House in Manor Top, Sheffield, sells pre-loved clothing, including coats, shoes, sportswear and school uniforms.

The project is run by Manor and Castle Development Trust in collaboration with community interest company Uni-Recycle, which collects and redistributes school uniforms at low prices.

Organisers said they wanted to make affordable clothing accessible to everyone while challenging the stigma sometimes associated with buying second-hand.

Manor and Castle Development Trust has been operating for almost 30 years and has about 45 members of staff.

Its work includes toddler groups, dementia support, physical health and mental wellbeing services, employment support, training and benefits advice.

Dawn Dale, the trust's community development manager, said the Echo project was named to reflect its aim of giving items a second life through reuse.

She said its low prices were designed to make clothing accessible to those who needed it, rather than to generate income.

She said the idea developed partly in response to the cost of living crisis and concerns about clothing going to landfill.

"We had a think about what we could do," she said.

"In our community there was quite a lot of stigma around second-hand clothing at that point."

Dale said brands such as John Lewis had helped the team create a boutique-style shop by advising on clothing displays and donating rails.

She said the aim was to create a shopping experience where people could find more than just school uniforms.

"While you're here looking for a school uniform, mum might see a jacket, dad might see some trainers," she said.

Dale also described York House as a place where people could meet, socialise and build friendships.

"You can come in and look for a blouse but actually while you are here you get offered a cup of tea, you can sit and do some crafting," she said.

"It break down barriers, it helps people build friendships."

As well as offering affordable, good-quality clothing, the Echo project on City Road helps people overcome barriers to taking part in physical activity.

The trust's chief executive, Lucy Warren, said the cost of trainers and gym wear could prevent some people from getting involved.

"We can, not only provide you something in the shop, but open up the opportunity for you to engage in lots of other ways," she said.

Kelly Anne Bell, also from the trust, runs the shops, which she said was about bringing people together and supporting the local community.

"This project supports so many families because school uniforms are so expensive," said Bell.

"We've had school uniforms coming in with the labels still on - for one dress it's £14 and we're offering [them for] 50p.

Shopper Kelly Prior said the project was needed in the community.

"I think it makes [people] feel more welcome in the area, knowing just a port of call where they can meet new people," she said.

"You can get everything here. I'm always a bargain hunter."

articles.body: Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal has shared a fresh update on the rollout of the Temple wearable device, announcing that pre-orders have now opened for users who had signed up for early access over the past few months. n a post, he told those users to check their mailboxes for details. Temple has attracted attention in India's startup ecosystem for its focus on tracking physiological and brain-related metrics. articles.title: The Oxfordshire blind musician singing in the face of adversity
articles.summary: Sardinian-born Elena Piras says her visual impairment is "part of my life, but it's not my life".
articles.body:
An award-winning singer, who was born with severely impaired vision, has said there is "so much that can be gained by inclusion and diversity".

Folk musician Elena Piras is originally from Sardinia, Italy, and now lives in Charlbury, Oxfordshire, where she has recorded her latest single.

In addition to her visual disability, she was also left with severe hearing loss after being caught up in the 7/7 London bombings in 2005.

Speaking to the BBC, she said she continues to pursue her music career despite the obstacles and is now fundraising for her third album.

Piras sang in choirs from the age of seven and has performed on national TV in Italy.

She said she came to England in 1995 at the age of 18, after finding out about The Royal National College for the Blind in Hereford.

"I knew that the opportunities for visually impaired people in my country were not amazing," she said. "We had very, very basic provision for anything and it was a fight to obtain it as well."

While her parents were "not very happy" about the move, Piras said she always wanted to be "as independent as possible".

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Piras said her visual impairment was "part of my life, but it's not my life", adding that people were "not even willing to listen to what I can do".

She said: "I really didn't know that there was a problem with me being blind and music, maybe my talent always gave me the bypass.

"People saw my visual impairment first and they still do. As soon as they discovered that, they closed their eyes.

"We have legislation in this country that should help, but it's not implemented and that is a real shame for everybody because there's so much that can be gained by inclusion and diversity in every single field."

On 7 July 2005, Piras was at King's Cross Station and heard the blast of the Piccadilly Line bomb as it detonated in the tunnel between the station and Russell Square.

She said: "It was just a nightmare day and I remember someone trying to put me in a taxi.

"The first taxi driver didn't want to travel to the area where I lived because it was too close."

Afterwards, she said she started to become "very irritated" in noisy places and had difficulty harmonising when she sang.

She moved to Scotland and a hearing test in Glasgow showed she had lost 60% of her hearing, she said, adding: "For someone who's visually impaired, that's a lot."

The musician went on to live in the Highlands, and later in the Shetlands, where she studied Scots and Gaelic traditional music.

She said: "I really wanted to learn it and I discovered that singing in a language, especially in Gaelic, it wasn't enough - I had to learn the language if I wanted to sing at a certain level.

"It was just incredible. I met so many amazing people and learned so much."

Piras said she "fell in love" in the feelings the music conveyed, as well as "the love for the land" and its traditions.

Her new single, recorded at Shaken Oak studios in Witney, Oxfordshire, is Shetland lullaby Baloo Balilli.

She said it was a song she learned in Shetland and the team behind her recording includes musicians such as Mercury Prize nominated drummer and percussionist Greig Stewart.

"We met for our rehearsal and this was the first song that we actually played together, almost straight away it was amazing," Piras said.

articles.title: In New Hampshire, Bob and Ruth Morrell turned more than 25 German storybook dolls into a village in 1954; Story Land now has more than 50 attractions
articles.summary: Discover the enchanting history of Story Land in New Hampshire, where a couple turned 25 German dolls into a beloved amusement park with over 30 attractions for children. Explore how they built a lasting family destination since 1954.
articles.body: Story Land in Glen, New Hampshire, grew from a collection of handmade storybook dolls into a theme park for young families. Its founders, Bob and Ruth Morrell, opened the park in late 1954 after dollmaker Frau Edith Von Arps suggested building a village around the figures. The Morrells expanded her idea to include storybook characters, rides and play areas. Story Land’s official history recounts how the idea developed. The park opened with a single ride, a fire engine that Bob drove with children as passengers. Over the decades, it added attractions such as Cinderella’s Pumpkin Coach and Castle in 1957 and continued expanding. Story Land now advertises more than 50 attractions, including rides, shows and play areas.A knock at the doorBob Morrell had been in the 10th Mountain Division of ski soldiers in the Second World War and had been recalled to service during the Korean Conflict. That took the pair to Germany, when an elderly woman named Frau Edith Von Arps showed up at their home. She was travelling from home to house selling dolls she had handcrafted, one for each classic children’s fairy tale.The Morrells became friends with Von Arps, who sold them more than 25 dolls before they returned to New Hampshire. She suggested that they build a small village around the dolls. The Morrells expanded the idea beyond a display, planning rides and play spaces where storybook creatures could live and characters could come to life.This was not their first rodeo in business. They owned the Eastern Slope Ice Cream Company in North Conway, the Concord Monitor reported. The park began with around $5,000, the New Hampshire Union Leader reported. They purchased a piece of land in Glen that the previous owner said wouldn’t even make a respectable pasture.Early years of riskThe park opened in late 1954, a year before Disneyland came up and transformed people’s expectations of amusement parks. According to the Conway Daily Sun, it was once called Story Town and had only one ride, a fire engine Bob drove with youngsters as passengers. Then came a few successful seasons, aided by the arrival of Cinderella’s Pumpkin Coach and Castle in 1957. Then the national economy stalled, and the fledgling park struggled. The local lenders didn’t want the mortgage on the home of the three bears, and the family got by working hard and giving money back into the park year after year. That habit paid off in the late 1960s. Bob bought an old German carousel in 1967 that still turns today, a train and a fleet of boats that became the Swan Boats. The Morrells had room to dream bigger, and visitors began to perceive the park as a location they wanted to return to.A park that kept growingThe 1970s were a busy decade. New additions included a chapel, a safari ride, a Moroccan bazaar, the first maze, a Dutch village with a shoe ride and a coaster that later became the Polar Coaster. The 1980s brought a pirate ship, a tea cup ride and a trip to the moon. The park’s latest new ride was a compact wooden coaster with a 40-foot drop, which opened in 2014. Its more recent major addition was Moo Lagoon, a water play area that debuted in 2024.The park continued as a family business through all this. Ruth handled the gift shop, Bob ran around making sure everyone was having fun, and their daughter Nancy played Mistress Mary in her garden as a child. Their son Stoney continued the work until he died in 2006, and the Morrell family ran the park until 2007, the Concord Monitor reported. Story Land continues to combine storybook settings with rides, shows and play areas for young visitors. The park’s official media information lists more than 50 attractions and describes its history of entertaining generations of families since opening in 1954.You use AI every day. articles.title: Family of 24 forced to get off a train over washrooms without water, paid extra to reach Shivamogga after railway staff failed to resolve their complaint, yet railways denied the problem until a consumer commission ordered a Rs 16,000 payout for deficiency in service
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Karnataka has held South Western Railway guilty of deficiency in service after a man travelling with 23
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Karnataka has held South Western Railway guilty of deficiency in service after a man travelling with 23 family members, including four children, had to get off a train because there was no water in the coach washrooms.The commission, in its October 17 order, directed the railway authorities to refund Rs 1,000 towards the original tickets, pay Rs 10,000 as compensation and Rs 5,000 towards litigation costs.Railway washroom disputeAccording to the commission’s order, the complainant, T Nagendra, a 52-year-old resident of Shivamogga, travelled with his wife, children and relatives to visit the Tirupati-Tirumala temples in Andhra Pradesh in April 2025.After leaving Tirupati on April 14, 2025, the family returned to Yeshwanthpura railway station in Bengaluru the following day to continue their journey to Shivamogga. The group, comprising 20 adults and four children, purchased second-class tickets worth Rs 1,000, from Yeshwanthpura to Shivamogga.However, after the train left Yeshwanthpura and proceeded towards Tumkur, the family members discovered that there was no water in the washrooms in their coach. The complainant alleged that the women and children in the group could not use the facilities because of the lack of water.Nagendra brought the problem to the attention of railway police personnel on duty in the train and sought help. However, according to the complaint, they were unable to resolve the issue and advised him to get off at Tumkur railway station and approach the station master.The complainant and his family members got off at Tumkur, where Nagendra lodged a written complaint with the station master on April 15, 2025. The complaint was acknowledged by the railway authorities.According to the complaint, the family then continued its journey to Shivamogga on another express train at around 8.30 pm after purchasing additional tickets worth Rs 1,760.Nagendra later sent a legal notice dated August 28, 2025, to the railway authorities, seeking a refund of the original ticket charges and compensation for the inconvenience and hardship suffered by the family. The authorities neither complied with the demand nor replied to the notice, according to the order.He approached the consumer commission seeking reimbursement of Rs 1,000 towards the original tickets, Rs 5 lakh for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, another Rs 5 lakh for hardship and mental agony, and Rs 5,000 towards legal and litigation expenses.The railway authorities denied the allegations. They claimed that the allegation about the absence of water in the coach was baseless and unsupported by evidence. They also said that water supply to coaches was ensured before trains departed from their originating stations and that the train had passenger amenities, including washrooms, water supply, electricity and fans.Commission’s findingThe bench comprising president T Shivanna and member B D Yogananda examined the railway tickets, the written complaint lodged at Tumkur station and other documents submitted by the complainant.The commission noted that the tickets and the acknowledged complaint supported Nagendra’s account that he and his family had travelled on April 15, 2025, before getting off at Tumkur because of the water problem in the washrooms. It also addressed the discrepancy in the year mentioned in the initial complaint, treating it as a typographical error in view of the supporting documents.“Whether a complaint by the Passenger/s is of much gravity and grave concern or even a trivial matter, the concerned Railway Authorities are duty bound to address/resolve the complaint in a suitable manner and a compliance/reply to be communicated to the complainant along with the details of the action taken on the complaint,” the bench observed.It noted that the railway authorities had failed to produce evidence to establish that there was no water supply problem in the coach. The commission also criticised their failure to respond to the complaint lodged at Tumkur and the subsequent legal notice.“The OPs nowhere in their pleadings have whispered anything about the complaint lodged by the complainant before the Station Master, Tumkur, vide Ex.P-14, which is the core issue that should have been addressed/resolved suitably by the OPs,” the commission said.The commission further noted that the railway authorities had focused on the incorrect year mentioned in the initial documents instead of addressing the passenger’s grievance. It held that the authorities had failed to rebut the evidence supporting the complaint.“For the foregoing discussions and the reasoning supra, this Commission is of the firm opinion that, the said acts of omission and commission by the OPs is nothing but, deficiency in service on their part towards the complainant and the grievances faced by the complainant,” it further added.Final orderPartly allowing the complaint, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Shivamogga, directed the two railway authorities to:Refund Rs 1,000 towards the original railway tickets, with 6 percent annual interest from April 15, 2025, if paid within 45 days.Pay Rs 10,000 as compensation for inconvenience, hardship and mental agony.Pay Rs 5,000 towards litigation costs.The total compensation and litigation costs amount to Rs 15,000, apart from the Rs 1,000 ticket refund.The commission directed the railway authorities to pay the compensation and litigation costs within 45 days of the order. If they fail to do so, these amounts will attract 10 percent annual interest from October 17, 2026, until payment. If the ticket refund is delayed beyond the stipulated period, it will carry 10 percent annual interest from April 15, 2025, until realisation.The commission did not award the Rs 10 lakh in compensation sought by the complainant, holding that the material on record did not justify such a large amount.

articles.title: Shruti Haasan calls Kamal Haasan her biggest ally: What psychology research reveals about raising independent children and why thinking for themselves matters more than making them agree with you
articles.summary: Children do not always grow up to share their parents’ opinions, choices or ideas about life.
articles.body: Children do not always grow up to share their parents’ opinions, choices or ideas about life. Sometimes, they question family traditions, challenge expectations and take paths their parents may not have imagined. But what if this independence is not a sign of failed parenting but evidence that children have learnt to think for themselves?Actor and musician Shruti Haasan offered an interesting perspective on this during a conversation with Twinkle Khanna at Tweak Summit 2026. Speaking about her bond with her father, actor Kamal Haasan, Shruti described him as her biggest ally since childhood. Her candid remarks offer a useful parenting takeaway: children need guidance and support, but they also need the freedom to develop an identity of their own.When a child’s independence reflects their upbringingTalking about her father’s influence, Shruti said, “My dad, he is really my biggest ally from my childhood which is the part of the reason I keep telling him I'm Frankenstein's monster. So everything that he disagrees with, I'm like, 'You raised me to be like this.’” Her humorous comparison points to a familiar experience in many families. Parents may encourage children to be confident, independent and willing to question the world, only to find that those same qualities sometimes lead their children to disagree with them.The important lesson is that independence should not automatically be mistaken for disrespect. A child who expresses a different opinion is not necessarily rejecting their parents. They may simply be applying the confidence and critical thinking they developed while growing up. Shruti’s description of Kamal as her ally is also significant. An ally is not someone who agrees with every decision, but someone who offers support and makes a person feel that they are not alone. For children, knowing that their parents will listen, even during disagreements, can create room for honest conversations.This does not mean parents must approve of every choice. They can establish boundaries, explain consequences and share their concerns while still respecting a child’s growing individuality. The aim is to guide children without making agreement the only acceptable response.What research says about giving children room to growShruti’s experience connects with a concept studied in psychology called parental autonomy support. It refers to the ways parents encourage children to develop their own opinions, make choices, understand their feelings and take increasing responsibility for their decisions, while still providing guidance and appropriate boundaries. A 2022 systematic review published in the 'Journal of Family Theory & Review' examined 63 studies on autonomy-supportive parenting. It found that this approach was associated with positive academic and social-emotional outcomes for children. The researchers also highlighted that family circumstances and cultural contexts influence how this kind of support is expressed.A separate meta-analysis published in 'Educational Psychology Review' examined 36 studies and found that parental autonomy support was associated with academic achievement and positive psychological outcomes, including motivation, perceived competence and psychological health. These findings suggest that giving children a voice can be valuable alongside providing structure and direction.For parents, this can begin with small everyday choices. Instead of immediately dismissing a child's opinion, ask why they feel that way. Explain the reasons behind household rules rather than relying only on “because I said so”. Allow age-appropriate decisions about hobbies, interests and personal expression. When disagreements arise, listen before responding. Importantly, supporting autonomy does not mean leaving children to manage everything alone. Children still need consistency, safety, emotional involvement and clear limits. The goal is to help them understand how to make thoughtful decisions, not simply to let them do whatever they want.Being a child’s ally does not mean agreeing with everythingDuring the conversation, Twinkle Khanna asked Shruti whether she was treated differently because she was Kamal Haasan’s daughter. Shruti responded, “He's always unimpressed with me. He's the standard Indian dad.” Her answer added humour to the discussion, but it also highlighted an important distinction: a parent can be supportive without constantly praising a child or agreeing with every choice. A healthy relationship can include disagreement, correction and high expectations, provided children still feel respected and valued.For Indian parents, this lesson can be especially relevant in families where educational choices, careers, relationships and personal decisions are often shaped by family expectations. Parents naturally want to protect their children from mistakes, but making every decision on their behalf can leave them with fewer opportunities to practise independent thinking. A more balanced approach is to remain involved while allowing children to participate in decisions that affect their lives. Parents can share their experience without assuming that their children must follow the same path. They can disagree without withdrawing affection, and they can correct behaviour without making a child feel that their entire identity is wrong.Shruti’s words do not offer a complete picture of her family’s parenting style, but they provide a relatable starting point for a wider conversation. Children learn from what parents teach them, but they also learn from the confidence, curiosity and independence that parents allow them to develop. Perhaps the lasting parenting lesson is this: raising a child is not about creating someone who always agrees with you. It is about helping them become someone who can think clearly, make responsible choices and still feel safe coming back to you, even when you disagree.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Israel election: Netanyahu bloc leads with more than half of votes counted but short of majority
articles.summary: The partial results are likely to change, and several exit polls showed the camps neck-and-neck without a majority.
articles.body:
The camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ahead of the opposition on Wednesday after 50% of votes were counted in Israel's pivotal general election, figures from the Central Elections Committee showed.

Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 56 of the 120 seats in the parliament, compared with 49 for the opposition bloc and 15 for the Arab parties.

The partial results are likely to change, and several exit polls showed the camps neck-and-neck without a majority.

Initial exit polls suggested no clear victor, with both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and main rival Gadi Eisenkot falling short of a majority.

Israel's Channel 13 news initially projected the opposition bloc would have the edge with 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, with Netanyahu's bloc set to win around 50.

The three mainstream Israeli television networks later gave the two blocs each around 51 seats.

Netanyahu's Likud party would be the largest single party, with 27 seats.

Israeli Arab lists were projected to win 15 seats, a sharp gain, with some Israeli Arab communities reporting near-universal turnout driven by outrage to often derogatory rhetoric against them by Netanyahu's far-right allies.

Key Israeli Arab leader Mansour Abbas said he believed the right had "suffered a major loss" and was open to working with Eisenkot.

But Eisenkot said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers -- and Netanyahu again suggested that a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.

Arab lawmakers could give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition. If not, Israel could head to new elections.

Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand who according to exit polls did not gain as much as many expected, warned Netanyahu against another option -- a unity government with Eisenkot.

"It would be a terrible mistake," said Ben Gvir, who champions the expulsion of Palestinians and would likely be excluded from any unity government.

In a post on X, Eisenkot said the exit poll results showed a "complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government."

Yair Golan, the leader of Israel's left-wing Democrats party, added that the public had "spoken" and "ousted the Netanyahu government."

But Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar warned that celebrations from the left were "premature."

"One thing seems quite clear: The Likud is the largest party in Israel," he wrote on social media.

Netanyahu and Eisenkot each claim mandate

At an appearance early Wednesday, Netanyahu was upbeat and already trying to position himself to remain prime minister, listing off military achievements of the past three years.

He called on his opponents to line up behind him and dismissed the idea of a partnership with Arab parties — whose constituents make up 20% of Israel's population — as treasonous.

"We must establish a strong, right-wing, nationalist government," said Netanyahu, who was facing off in the vote against his former military chief, centrist Gadi Eisenkot. "We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

"Israel has a unique opportunity with our partner President Trump to forever eliminate the existential threat of Iran," Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot, speaking to his own supporters in Tel Aviv, issued a veiled warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use a war to push for a unity government.

"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.

Addressing Israel's security establishment, Eisenkot said that they served the state and not Netanyahu, calling him "a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust".

Turnout for the election - Israel's first since Hamas' 7 October 2023 attacks - hit over 77%, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.

Netanyahu had spent much of the day calling on supporters to get out and vote, painting the election as a "matter of life and death."

The vote is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership.

articles.title: Princess Diana's secret love story: She wanted to marry a heart surgeon she trusted most, saying, ‘Everybody sells me out. He is the one person who will never sell me out’
articles.summary: Princess Diana reportedly wanted to marry Pakistani heart surgeon Hasnat Khan, with whom she had a relationship lasting nearly two years before her death
articles.body: Princess Diana reportedly wanted to marry Pakistani heart surgeon Hasnat Khan, with whom she had a relationship lasting nearly two years before her death in August 1997. Their romance remained largely private, away from the intense media attention surrounding the Princess of Wales. Diana believed Khan was different from the people who had disappointed her, telling a friend in the summer of 1997: “Everybody sells me out. Hasnat is the one person who will never sell me out.” The quotation appeared in a 2013 Vanity Fair investigation by journalist Sarah Ellison, which drew on interviews with people close to Diana. Their relationship was shaped by her hopes for a future together and Khan's concerns about the consequences of living in the public eye.How Princess Diana met Hasnat KhanDiana met Khan on September 1, 1995, at London's Royal Brompton Hospital, where he was working as a cardiac surgeon. She had visited a friend, Oonagh Toffolo, whose husband was receiving treatment following heart surgery. Khan came to the waiting room to discuss the patient's condition, and Toffolo introduced him to Diana.According to the account later published in Vanity Fair, Khan's professional manner and apparent indifference to Diana's celebrity made an impression on her. She returned to the hospital during her friend's husband's stay, and the two gradually developed a relationship.Their romance continued for around two years. They spent time together privately, including at Kensington Palace and Khan's home in Chelsea, sometimes taking precautions to avoid photographers. Diana's friends later described the relationship as one of the most significant in her life after her marriage to then-Prince Charles.Princess Diana wanted to marry the heart surgeonDiana's feelings for Khan reportedly went beyond a private romance. According to Jemima Khan, a close friend who was married to Imran Khan, a distant cousin of the surgeon, Diana was deeply in love with Hasnat and wanted to marry him, even if it meant living in Pakistan.Diana reportedly sought Jemima's advice about what life with a Pakistani husband might involve. During visits to Pakistan in 1996 and 1997, Diana also met members of Khan's family and explored the possibility of a future together. Her interest in marriage was also discussed during the inquest into her death in 2008.Former royal butler Paul Burrell told the inquest that Diana had asked him whether a private marriage between a Christian and a Muslim could be arranged. He said she had described Khan as her soulmate and the man she loved more than any other.‘Everybody sells me out’: Diana trusted Hasnat KhanThis quotation appeared in Sarah Ellison's September 2013 Vanity Fair article, which examined Diana's relationship with Khan through interviews with people who knew them.Ellison reported that Diana told a friend during the summer of 1997: “Everybody sells me out. Hasnat is the one person who will never sell me out.”The words reflected the trust Diana reportedly placed in Khan during a period when her private life attracted intense public scrutiny. The surgeon was not part of the royal establishment or celebrity world, and he appeared to offer her a relationship in which she could spend time away from her public role.The quotation is a retrospective account attributed to Diana by the magazine, rather than a statement preserved in a contemporaneous recording or transcript. It nevertheless became a defining detail in later accounts of the relationship and Khan's preference for privacy.Why their relationship eventually endedDespite their feelings for each other, Diana and Khan faced a fundamental disagreement about what a shared future would look like. Diana was one of the most recognisable women in the world, while Khan wanted to continue his medical career without becoming a permanent subject of press attention.In his statement to the inquest into Diana's death, Khan said his main concern about marriage was that his life would be “hell because of who she was”. He worried that constant media scrutiny would prevent them from leading a normal life, including if they had children.He also described receiving anonymous threats during their relationship, including envelopes containing cut-out pictures of him with a noose around his neck. The threats added to the stress of a relationship already complicated by publicity.Khan said the relationship ended after Diana returned from a holiday in the south of France in the summer of 1997 and told him it was over. The breakup came shortly before her relationship with Dodi Al Fayed became prominent in the press.Hasnat Khan's life away from the spotlightKhan largely maintained his privacy after Diana's death on August 31, 1997. He did provide information to investigators and later addressed aspects of their relationship in connection with the inquest, but he did not collaborate with the 2013 film Diana, starring Naomi Watts.He also criticised the film's portrayal of their relationship, saying the filmmakers had got it wrong. In interviews, he described Diana and himself as friends who interacted as normal people, rather than through the hierarchy associated with her royal status.His reluctance to turn the relationship into a public narrative contrasted with the sustained attention it attracted after Diana's death. Their romance remains part of the story of her private life, but the most intimate details largely come from accounts by friends, associates and people who later spoke to journalists.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'The whole tide turned': Trump takes credit for Netanyahu's showing in Israel elections
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump has claimed that his endorsement helped Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu turn the tide in Israel’s 26th Knesset
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has claimed that his endorsement helped Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu turn the tide in Israel’s 26th Knesset election, contributing to the incumbent’s better-than-expected performance. Partial results showed Netanyahu’s bloc leading the race but falling short of the majority needed to form a government.With 57.3% of ballot boxes counted as of 7:58 am, partial results released by the Central Elections Committee showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc securing 55 seats, against 49 for the anti-Netanyahu bloc. Arab parties were projected to win 16 seats.Meanwhile, Reservists, with 2.6% of the vote, People of Israel, with 1.7%, and Charedi Public, with 0.2%, remained below the 3.25% electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset. Votes cast in double envelopes, including those of soldiers, are counted later.On Wednesday, Trump took to Truth Social, where he shared comments by Irving C Schwartz, “When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu."It all took place AFTER the Endorsement by President Trump, who only wants what is good for the Middle East, Israel, and the United States of America!”Additionally, The Jerusalem Post reported that, while speaking to reporters on the tarmac near Air Force One after attending a rally in Texas, Trump said the Israeli leader had exceeded expectations.“I heard the poll numbers were wrong..., the exit polls; I heard he [Netanyahu] did very well. It was pretty close, but very well. When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said.He added, “It's a little bit early, but I'm hearing in Israel, top people say, 'Wow! He did a lot better than people thought.' It's looking like maybe a stalemate or a win.”The remarks came after Netanyahu publicly highlighted Trump’s support ahead of the election. In a televised appearance late on Sunday night, the Israeli prime minister praised the US president’s backing.“US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again,” Netanyahu said.“He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me.”Trump had urged Israelis to back Netanyahu in a social media post on Sunday, writing: “Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!”Netanyahu also suggested that the two countries could take further action against Iran, saying Trump was willing to act “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat”. He added that he had instructed Israel’s intelligence agency, Mossad, and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to pursue regime change in Iran.Meanwhile, the exit polls suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s each won about 51 seats, and Arab parties won about 18. Netanyahu called for a right-wing government, claiming his bloc had a “significant, decisive majority” among Jewish voters and those supporting a Jewish state.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, Andhra Pradesh's Singampalli Parwathi borrowed Rs 20,000 to trade raw cashews; today she processes 11 grades of cashew kernels and reports annual business turnover near Rs 50 lakh
articles.summary: In 2018, Singampalli Parwathi borrowed Rs 20,000 to begin buying and selling raw cashew nuts in Natavaram village in Andhra Pradesh’s Anakapalli district.
articles.body: In 2018, Singampalli Parwathi borrowed Rs 20,000 to begin buying and selling raw cashew nuts in Natavaram village in Andhra Pradesh’s Anakapalli district. Eight years later, her business has grown into a cashew-processing enterprise with an annual turnover of around Rs 50 lakh, according to the Press Information Bureau (PIB).Parwathi’s journey began when she was looking for a way to improve her family’s financial situation. According to a PIB report, her household depended on a small farm, two dairy buffaloes and her husband’s daily-wage earnings. The income was often insufficient to meet household expenses and unexpected costs, forcing the family to borrow money at high interest rates.She wanted to start a business of her own, but a lack of capital stood in her way. Joining the Sri Durga Bhavani Farmer Producer Group in 2018 gave her access to a small loan and a starting point for her enterprise.From trading raw cashews to processing kernelsThe initial Rs 20,000 loan allowed Parwathi to buy and sell raw cashew nuts. The business helped her understand the market and identify an opportunity to earn more by processing the nuts herself. In 2019, she obtained another loan of Rs 50,000. According to the PIB report, she used the money to purchase two cutting machines and began extracting cashew kernels, which she sold to traders in Tuni. Moving into processing meant she was no longer limited to trading raw cashews. It also gave her an opportunity to add value to the produce before selling it.As the business expanded, Parwathi needed more equipment and working capital. The farmer producer group continued to support her, providing a loan of Rs 2 lakh. She also secured Rs 3 lakh in bank financing under the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP). Together, the funds helped her establish a larger cashew-processing unit, according to the PIB account.Her business now processes 11 grades of cashewParwathi now processes cashews into 11 different grades to meet varying customer requirements. She supplies her products to customers across India and participates in exhibitions to display and sell her products, according to the PIB report. Her enterprise has reached an annual turnover of approximately Rs 50 lakh. This is the reported turnover of the business, not its profit; the report does not specify how much she earns after operating expenses.The growth from a Rs 20,000 initial loan to a business with this level of turnover illustrates how access to credit helped her move from buying and selling raw produce to running a processing unit.How a farmer producer group helped her expandThe Sri Durga Bhavani Farmer Producer Group played a central role in Parwathi’s business journey by connecting her to credit at different stages. The first loan helped her enter the trade, the second enabled her to buy machinery, and further group and bank financing supported the expansion of her processing operations.Her story is included in a PIB feature on women entrepreneurs whose businesses are being showcased at the National SARAS Mela 2026 in Vijayawada. The event brings together rural enterprises and self-help group-linked businesses, giving participants a platform to display and sell their products.Parwathi’s business has grown through successive investments rather than a single large loan. She began with raw cashew trading, added machinery the following year and later secured funds to expand processing. Today, she supplies graded kernels to customers across the country.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: After Oregon governor bans datacenters across the state over environmental permits; City council declares 'state of emergency'; warns residents: This will disrupt …
articles.summary: A city in Oregon has declared a state of emergency after the governor’s restrictions on new data centre projects threatened about $6 million in expected
articles.body: A city in Oregon has declared a state of emergency after the governor’s restrictions on new data centre projects threatened about $6 million in expected revenue. Umatilla officials warned that the move could delay public infrastructure projects, affect jobs and put billions of dollars in planned private investment at risk. The emergency declaration follows Oregon Governor Tina Kotek’s decision to suspend new environmental permits for data centres until July 2027. Umatilla officials say the restrictions could affect planned developments in the city, where data centres have become an important source of expected future revenue.Why Oregon city council declared emergencyUmatilla’s city council approved the emergency declaration over concerns that the state’s restrictions could disrupt its financial plans. The city had included expected data centre revenue in future budgets, with some of the money intended for infrastructure improvements.The projects at risk include a proposed police station and several million dollars in upgrades to the city’s water infrastructure. City Manager Dave Stockdale warned that delays in receiving the expected payments could force officials to reconsider the timelines for these projects.However, the city said it is not facing an immediate budget crisis. The money has not yet been received or spent, and existing public services and financial obligations remain unaffected.Data centre restrictions put billions in investment at riskUmatilla currently has four operational data centres, while another facility is under construction and two more developments are awaiting completion. Companies operating in the area include Amazon Web Services and Sabey Data Centers. According to the city’s estimates, the restrictions could put more than $5 billion in planned private investment at risk. Officials also warned that at least 1,000 construction jobs, along with hundreds of permanent jobs and other employment opportunities, could be affected.Some projects awaiting regulatory approval could face delays of more than two years. Developers may also abandon their plans or move their investments to other locations, the city warned.“These consequences extend far beyond the interests of individual businesses. They threaten the broader economic and financial well-being of the Umatilla community,” said Dave Stockdale, Umatilla city manager.What are Oregon’s restrictions on data centresIn October, Kotek directed Oregon’s environmental authorities to suspend new pollution permits for data centres, effectively restricting new development until July 2027. The governor had also halted transactions involving state-owned land intended for data centre projects while officials reviewed their potential long-term effects.The move followed an August decision to block the sale of 32 acres at Salem’s Mill Creek Corporate Center for a proposed Verrus development. Other local authorities have introduced restrictions as well. Hillsboro, for example, imposed a 120-day pause on new data centre developments in July 2026.Umatilla’s emergency resolution calls for the situation to be reviewed within 90 days. It also authorises an assessment of the possible financial and employment losses and urges the governor to reconsider the restrictions. articles.title: Knife-wielding attacker shot dead outside Israeli embassy in Serbia
articles.summary: A knife-wielding assailant was shot dead after attacking a security guard outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade shortly after midnight on Wednesday,
articles.body: A knife-wielding assailant was shot dead after attacking a security guard outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade shortly after midnight on Wednesday, Serbian police said.Serbian interior minister Ivica Dacic said authorities were investigating the incident as a “terrorist attack”. The government raised the terror threat level to its highest category and increased security at key locations across the country, according to the news agency AP.According to Dacic, the attacker was a minor and was carrying two knives. He allegedly shouted “Allahu Akbar”, meaning “God is great” in Arabic, while attacking a member of Serbia’s Gendarmerie guarding the embassy.The officer sustained a minor facial injury but managed to shoot and kill the assailant in self-defence, the minister said.Photographs released by police showed the security booth outside the embassy, with the surrounding area cordoned off using police tape. Armed officers in tactical gear were seen at the scene.Dacic said the attacker was believed to have come from Sabac, a town in western Serbia. He added that security agencies had been monitoring the individual, whom he described as a supporter of the Islamic State group.“He kept the black flag in support of the Islamic State on his Instagram account,” Dacic said.Attack follows political upheaval in Serbia and IsraelThe incident occurred days after Serbia held an early parliamentary election on Sunday, following nearly two years of protests against former president Aleksandar Vucic and his long-standing political leadership. A youth-led movement emerged as a major force in the election, although Vucic and his allies continue to control the police while the formation of a new government remains pending.Israel also held a parliamentary election on Tuesday, with exit polls indicating that no clear winner had emerged.The latest incident follows a similar attack outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade in June 2024. articles.title: Tamil Nadu jailbreak: Armed personnel to guard 9 central prisons, 5 women’s prisons and 13 district jails round the clock
articles.summary: CHENNAI: In a sweeping security overhaul following the escape of 17 prisoners from Theni sub-jail, the prisons department has deployed personnel armed
articles.body: CHENNAI: In a sweeping security overhaul following the escape of 17 prisoners from Theni sub-jail, the prisons department has deployed personnel armed with self-loading rifles (SLRs) to guard watchtowers round the clock at nine central prisons, five special prisons for women and 13 district jails.Personnel have been instructed to open fire at inmates attempting to escape.The move comes as the department steps up security across the state to prevent a repeat of the jailbreak. It has also cancelled personnel’s leave, directed them to report for duty immediately and instructed them to carry batons.Highly placed sources said the department had issued SLRs to Tamil Nadu Special Police personnel and prison staff assigned to guard watchtowers along prison perimeters.“Every central and district prison has five to six watchtowers. These will be manned round the clock by personnel armed with SLRs to thwart escape attempts. They have also been instructed to open fire if any prisoner attempts to escape,” a senior prison official said.The weapons were issued from the department’s armoury on Tuesday. Armed personnel began guarding watchtowers at central prisons the same day, with the arrangement extended to district jails from Wednesday.Director general of prisons and correctional services Sandeep Rai Rathore has issued clear instructions to “open fire at prisoners attempting to escape”, the official said.However, Rathore said the deployment would depend on security requirements and the prevailing situation.“Depending on the security requirements and prevailing situation, watchtower personnel will be armed as a preventive measure. A security audit of prisons has been underway for the past week. Once the audit reports are received by the end of this month, a gap analysis will be carried out and further decisions will be taken to strengthen prison security and address vulnerabilities,” he said.The department has also issued a standard operating procedure (SOP) to prevent jailbreaks and prisoner escapes as part of the wider security measures.Tamil Nadu has 125 prison institutions, including nine central prisons, five special prisons for women, 13 district jails, 82 sub-jails for men, two special sub-jails each for men and women, three open-air prisons and a young offender correctional facility.The total authorised capacity is 24,148 inmates.Although the prison population is around 23,600, below the state’s overall authorised capacity, overcrowding remains a concern because inmates are unevenly distributed across facilities.Central prisons in Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai, along with several district prisons in southern Tamil Nadu, are operating at 115% to 150% of their sanctioned capacity, adding to security challenges.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news.
